Hi Priya,

I'm Renata Alvarez, an ICU nurse moving into clinical implementation work. Fennel & Finch delivers care virtually, and I want to help clinical teams adopt new systems and virtual care platforms. I don't know of an open role, so I'm writing about the team and roles to come.

At Mission Trail, I was an Epic super-user during the hospital's move from paper and Meditech. I trained an estimated 60 nurses in the Epic practice environment before go-live. More recently, I was one of six nurses piloting virtual nursing on a 28-bed med-surg unit, and I wrote most of the shared workflow documentation.

Would you be open to a short call about how your team works and what roles may come up?

Renata Alvarez

followUps.subject: Clinical Implementation Specialist (RN) application
followUps.text:
Hello Dana,

I applied today, October 6, for the Clinical Implementation Specialist (RN) role on your team. I wanted to write to you directly because the posting asks for a nurse who has lived through a go-live from the unit side, and I have.

When Mission Trail moved to Epic, I was one of about 40 super-users. Before go-live I trained an estimated 60 ICU, step-down, and float pool nurses in the Epic practice environment. During launch I gave three weeks of at-the-elbow support and kept a log of roughly 150 workflow problems and build defects so we could track each one to a fix.

Could you tell me what the next step in your process looks like, and roughly when to expect it? I would be glad to talk with you or anyone on the team about the role.

Thank you for your time.

Renata Alvarez

# icu-staffing-dashboard

A nurse-to-patient ratio dashboard for hospital inpatient units, built as my capstone for the Google Data Analytics Professional Certificate (finished June 2026).

It answers the question a charge nurse asks every shift: **given the census and acuity on each unit, where are we going to be short, and by how many nurses?**

> **All data in this repo is synthetic.** There is no patient data and no data from any real hospital. The numbers were generated in Google Sheets to look like a realistic month on four units.

## What it shows

- Nurse-to-patient ratio by unit and by shift (07:00–19:00 days, 19:00–07:00 nights)
- Acuity-weighted ratio next to the raw ratio, so a unit with three high-acuity patients doesn't look "fine" just because the headcount works
- Shifts where a unit went over its target ratio, color coded red / yellow / green
- How many extra nurses each unit would have needed per shift to stay at target
- A simple trend of over-ratio shifts across the month

The live dashboard is in Looker Studio (link in `docs/dashboard-link.md`). Screenshots are in `docs/screenshots/`.

## Repo layout

```
data/
  units.csv            # 4 units: ICU, step-down, med-surg, ED hold
  shifts.csv           # 31 days x 2 shifts x 4 units
  census.csv           # patients per unit per shift, with acuity level 1-4
  staffing.csv         # RNs scheduled vs. RNs actually worked per shift
sql/
  01_clean.sql         # trims, fixes the date formats, drops duplicate rows
  02_ratios.sql        # raw and acuity-weighted ratios per unit per shift
  03_gaps.sql          # nurses short vs. target ratio
  04_summary.sql       # monthly rollup used by the dashboard
docs/
  capstone-writeup.md  # the case study for the certificate
  screenshots/
```

## How to run it

You don't need to install anything. Everything runs in free tools.

1. Create a free BigQuery sandbox project in Google Cloud.
2. Make a dataset called `staffing` and upload the four CSVs in `data/` as tables with the same names.
3. Open each file in `sql/` in the BigQuery editor and run them in order (01 → 04). Each one writes a new table into the `staffing` dataset.
4. In Looker Studio, add a data source pointing at `staffing.summary` and `staffing.gaps`.
5. Make a copy of the dashboard from the link in `docs/dashboard-link.md` and swap in your data source.

If you just want to look, the screenshots and the write-up are enough.

## Design notes

**Target ratios.** I used common targets as defaults: ICU 1:2, step-down 1:3, med-surg 1:5, ED hold 1:4. They live in `units.csv` so you can change them without touching the SQL.

**Acuity weighting.** Each patient has an acuity level from 1 (stable) to 4 (unstable, needs 1:1). The weighted census counts a level 4 as 2 patients and a level 3 as 1.5. That's a rough rule I picked from my own charge nurse experience, not a validated acuity tool, and the write-up says so.

**Scheduled vs. worked.** The gap that matters at 4 a.m. is between who was scheduled and who actually showed up, so `staffing.csv` keeps both. The dashboard uses "worked."

**Why Looker Studio.** The course taught Tableau, but Looker Studio connects straight to BigQuery, it's free, and anyone with the link can view it without an account. That mattered for showing it to non-technical people.

**What I'd change.** Real staffing data would come out of a scheduling system, not CSVs, and float nurses would need their own handling. I left float pool out to keep the capstone a reasonable size.

## Status

Done as a capstone (June 2026). I'm not actively adding features. It has never been connected to real hospital data and shouldn't be without the right approvals.

Issues and suggestions are welcome, especially from other nurses who've had to staff a unit off a whiteboard.

## License

MIT

narrativeVersions.body:
What I want next. I want to get off the bedside and into the side of healthcare where you figure out how the work should flow. I've been a nurse for twelve years and the parts I loved most were never the procedures. It was being charge and solving the puzzle, being the Epic super-user and translating between the nurses and the people building the system, and the virtual nursing pilot, where we had to invent the workflow from nothing.

So the jobs I'm looking at: clinical implementation, like an implementation specialist or clinical implementation consultant at an EHR company or a virtual care company, the person who helps a hospital or clinic actually go live and get their nurses using the thing. Or clinical operations, especially for virtual care or telehealth, running the nurse side of a virtual program, the workflows, the staffing, the metrics. Clinical informatics would be great too, I know that's harder to get into without Epic certification, but I'd take a nurse informaticist or clinical analyst role in a heartbeat if someone would sponsor the cert.

Companies that excite me are the ones doing virtual care or digital health that actually touches patients and clinicians, places like Quillfield, Bellwick, Medlattice, Dosewell, Fennel & Finch. I want a company that has nurses in the room when they decide things, not one that thinks nurses are just users.

What I don't want. I don't want to go back to full-time bedside. Part-time PRN on the side maybe, but not as my main job. I don't want sales. I've had device reps tell me I'd be great at it and I'm sure I'd make money, but I'm not carrying a quota and I'm not selling to my old coworkers. No clinical sales, no medical device sales, no "clinical account executive" that's really sales with a nursing title. And I'm not trying to become a software engineer. I took one SQL course. I like data and I'll use it, but I'm not going to be a developer and I don't want to pretend.

The hard stuff, plainly:

Pay. I need at least $95,000 base. Below that, honestly, I'm better off picking up more shifts as a nurse, so anything under $95k base is a no, I don't care how cool the company is.

Location. I live in Denver and I'm staying in Denver. Daniel's job is here and we bought a house. So it's hybrid in the Denver area or fully remote anywhere in the US. I won't relocate, and I'm not doing something that's onsite four days a week in another city either.

Travel. I can travel some, I know implementation means go-lives, but at most about 25%, so like a week a month on average. Not a road warrior job. I did that with travel nursing.

Work authorization. I'm a US citizen, so no sponsorship needed, and I don't have any kind of security clearance, I've never needed one.

Other than that I'm flexible. I'd take a step down in title if it gets me into the right company. I'd like to stay close enough to patients that I remember why it matters.

narrativeVersions.body:
Okay so right now I'm at Foothill Peaks Medical Center here in Denver. I'm part-time, which honestly I never thought I'd say, I was always the one picking up extra shifts. I'm 0.6, so two twelves a week, 24 hours, mostly in the ICU. It's a mixed medical-surgical ICU, and sometimes they float me to step-down when they're short, which is a lot.

How I got here. We moved up from San Antonio in March 2022 because Daniel, my partner, got a job offer here, he's a civil engineer, and it was too good for him to pass up. I'd been off work for a while at that point, after the travel nursing stuff, so the timing kind of worked out. I didn't actually start at Foothill Peaks until July 2022 because the license transfer took forever. Well, Texas and Colorado are both compact states so it shouldn't have, but there was some issue with my address change and the background check. Anyway. July 2022.

The part-time thing was on purpose. I knew I didn't want to go back to full-time bedside. I love my patients, I do, but my back, and also I think after COVID I just can't do three or four twelves a week anymore and still be a person. So I took part-time and kept the other days for figuring out what's next.

The thing I'm proudest of here honestly isn't even the nursing part. When I started, our unit's staffing was done on a paper grid and a whiteboard, and the charge nurse would be texting people at four in the morning trying to fill holes. I built a Google Sheet, a staffing grid, where the charge enters census and acuity, and it shows where we're going to be short over the next 24 hours and color codes it, red, yellow, green. My manager liked it and now she pulls it up every morning for our unit huddle. I think it saves her like an hour a day? She said that once, I didn't time it. I'd honestly say my sheet is basically how the hospital does staffing now. Which, okay, it's mostly our unit. A couple of other managers asked for a copy, but I don't know if they actually use it.

The other big thing was the virtual nursing pilot in 2024. The hospital was trying out having a nurse work remotely, from a little office with a camera and a screen in the patient rooms, doing admissions, discharge teaching, med reconciliation, all the documentation stuff, so the bedside nurses could actually be at the bedside. They picked six of us bedside nurses to pilot it and I was one of them. It was for a 28-bed med-surg unit, not my ICU. I did it for about four months, so two of my shifts a week were virtual instead of ICU. I really liked it. I liked figuring out the workflow, like what the virtual nurse owns and what the bedside nurse owns, who signs what, and we kept a shared doc of everything that was breaking. I think I wrote most of that doc, honestly. Discharge teaching got way more consistent, the bedside nurses said they had more time, and I think the discharges-before-noon number went up but I never saw the final report. The pilot ended when the grant money ran out, or that's what we were told, I'm not totally sure. They said they'd revisit it in 2026 and so far, no.

That pilot is what made me look at the operations side of healthcare. I realized I like the part where you figure out how the work should flow more than I like doing the twelfth bath of the night. Sorry, that sounds bad. You know what I mean.

So last September, September 2025, I started the Google Data Analytics certificate. Spreadsheets, SQL, a bit of R which I did not love, Tableau, and I ended up doing my capstone in Looker Studio because it was free and easy to share. I finished in June 2026. For the capstone I did a staffing ratio dashboard, nurse-to-patient ratios by shift against census and acuity, on made-up data, because obviously I can't use real patient stuff. It's on my GitHub. It's not fancy, but I actually understand what a join is now, which a year ago, no way.

Oh, and I'm on the unit practice council here, we meet once a month, I've been on it since 2023. We redid how we do bedside shift report, that was most of last year. That's about it for here, I think.

narrativeVersions.body:
The Epic go-live. So I basically ran the Epic rollout at Mission Trail. That's how it felt anyway, ha.

Okay, more accurately. Mission Trail Health switched from the old system to Epic in October 2017. The old system was Meditech, I think, some really old version of it, half the ICU stuff was still on paper flowsheets. The whole system went live at once, big bang, all the hospitals and the clinics the same weekend. There was a whole project team for it, people from Epic, consultants, our IT people, the informatics nurses. I was not on that team. What they did was pick super-users from every unit, and I was one of the super-users for the MICU. There were about 40 of us across the hospital, I think, maybe a few more if you count the clinics.

How I got picked is kind of funny. Our manager asked who was good with computers and everybody looked at me because I was the one who fixed the printer. That's honestly it.

Before go-live we did super-user training, a few full days, and then we had to know our unit's workflows cold. The actual end-user classes were taught by the credentialed trainers, but the super-users ran the practice labs on our units, in the sandbox, the playground environment they called it. I ran those for our nurses, and then they added the step-down nurses and some of the float pool because step-down's super-user went on maternity leave. So I trained about 60 nurses in total, I think. Sixty-ish. I made cheat sheets for the drip titration documentation because that was the thing everyone was scared of, and the cheat sheets ended up being passed around to the other ICUs, which I was kind of proud of.

I kept an issue log, a spreadsheet, of everything that broke or confused people on our unit, and I think it got to around 150 items by the end of the three weeks. Some were real build problems, like the ICU drip flowsheet rows were missing a couple of our concentrations, and some were just training stuff. I'd send the real ones to the command center and track them till they got fixed. A lot of the build problems I logged did get fixed, which felt good, because a lot of people thought nobody was listening.

I also wasn't charge yet at that point, that came later, I got charge in 2019. So I didn't have any official authority on the unit, I was just a staff nurse in an orange vest telling older nurses where to click. That was its own kind of hard.

After go-live I stayed on as the unit super-user. We had a monthly super-user meeting for about a year, where we brought optimization requests, stuff the units wanted changed. I put in a bunch for the ICU, the sepsis alert stuff later came partly out of that relationship with the informatics team, I knew who to email.

Honestly this is the part of my career I think about the most now. I didn't know clinical informatics was a job when I was in school. The informatics nurses at Mission Trail were like, you should apply when there's an opening, and there was one opening in 2019 but it wanted Epic certification and you can only get that if your employer sponsors you, and they gave it to someone internal from IT. So I didn't go for it. Kind of regret that.

But what I learned is I'm good at being the person in between. Between the nurses and the people building the thing. I can translate what the nurse means into what the analyst needs to fix, and I can explain to a scared nurse why the screen works the way it does. I think that's the actual skill. And I like it more than I thought I would.
narrativeVersions.title: Epic go-live at Mission Trail

narrativeVersions.body:
Travel nursing. I left Mission Trail in June 2020 and signed with Lonestar Traveler Staffing, which is a travel agency out of Houston, small, but my recruiter there was honestly great. I did travel ICU from July 2020 to August 2021. I've worked in like ten different hospitals because of it, it feels like, you lose track.

Okay actually let me count. It was four contracts. First one was Laredo, Texas, July to October 2020, a community hospital, their ICU was maybe 16 beds and they had turned a med-surg floor into overflow ICU too. Then El Paso, October 2020 into January 2021, I extended that one. El Paso was the worst thing I've ever seen as a nurse. That was the fall surge, they had the refrigerated trucks outside. Ratios were one to three, some nights one to four with vented patients, which is not safe, everybody knew it was not safe, and we did it anyway. The pay was the most I'll ever make as a nurse, I think it peaked around $4,800 a week, and I'd give it back. Well. Maybe not all of it.

Then Bakersfield, California, February to May 2021. California has the mandated ratios so it was one to two, it felt like a vacation compared to El Paso, which is a messed up thing to say about an ICU during COVID. And the last one was Tulsa, Oklahoma, May to August 2021. In Tulsa they actually had me in charge some shifts, which travelers usually don't get, because they were so short on core staff with experience. So four hospitals, four cities.

You get a four-hour orientation if you're lucky, and then you have patients. I got really fast at figuring out how a place actually works, like who really decides things, where the supplies are hidden, which doctor you call versus which one you page. I used to make myself a one-page cheat sheet for each hospital the first night. I still have them somewhere.

I also noticed every place was having the same problems. Staffing, obviously. But also the documentation, the handoffs, the same alerts everyone clicks through. Every hospital thought its mess was special, and it really wasn't.

By August 2021 I was done. Like, done done. I was having trouble sleeping, I'd hear the vent alarms when I was in the grocery store. I didn't renew in Tulsa and I went home to San Antonio. And then my mom had her hip replacement that October, she lives alone, so I moved back in with her for a few months and took care of her through the recovery and the PT. So I just didn't work. I took a real break, the first time since nursing school. Daniel was still in San Antonio then, this is before he got the Denver job. Then he got the offer in early 2022 and we moved to Denver in March 2022, and I didn't go back to work until July 2022 when I started at Foothill Peaks. So it was about ten or eleven months off, start to finish, September 2021 to July 2022.

Nobody asked me to, it just happened. I made them the same cheat sheet I made for myself. I think I did that for maybe eight or ten nurses over those three months. It wasn't official at all, but they had me do it again in Tulsa.
narrativeVersions.title: Travel nursing with Lonestar Traveler Staffing

narrativeVersions.body:
My first job out of school. I graduated with my BSN in May 2014 from Bexar Valley College of Nursing, passed boards that July, and started at Mission Trail Regional Medical Center in August 2014 in their new grad residency. They put me on 5 West, which is a 32-bed med-surg unit. Mostly medical, some post-op, lots of COPD and heart failure and diabetic foot stuff, and a lot of elderly patients who fall. I did nights the whole first year because that's what new grads got.

Ratios were one to five on days and one to six on nights, sometimes seven when someone called out, which was a lot. Honestly med-surg is where you learn time management or you drown. I learned to chart fast and prioritize. I also learned I was really bad at saying no to people, which, still working on it.

The thing from 5 West I'd actually put on paper is the falls work. Our unit had one of the worst fall rates in the hospital, and in 2015 I joined the unit falls committee. It was me, two other nurses, a tech, and our nurse manager would come sometimes. We did hourly rounding with a script, the four Ps, pain, potty, position, possessions, and we got the bed alarms actually turned on, because people were turning them off since they went off all the time, and the yellow socks and wristbands for high-risk patients. I made the hourly rounding log that went on the door. Falls went down, I think from like five a month to two or three, I don't remember exactly, our manager had the numbers. It's not like we fixed falls forever, but it was better.

I also precepted. After my first year they had me precept new grads, and I precepted six of them between 2015 and 2016. I liked it a lot. I was basically the unit educator for a while there. Well, not officially, we had an actual clinical educator for 5 West and a couple of other units, she ran the skills fairs and the competencies, but she was spread really thin so I helped her with the skills fair once and people came to me with questions. I liked being the person people asked.

I got moved to days in 2015, I think that summer. Days were busier but I had more interaction with the doctors and case management and that's where I first got a feel for discharges and bed flow, like why a patient who's medically ready to go still sits there for two days waiting on a nursing home bed. That stuff always frustrated me. Nobody owned it.

I left 5 West in June 2016 to go to the MICU. I'd been wanting ICU since school, and the hospital had an internal ICU internship, a few months of classes and precepted shifts, so I applied and got in. My manager on 5 West was sad, she said she'd hoped I'd go into charge there. But I wanted the ICU.

Looking back, med-surg gave me the basics. And honestly I think it made me good at the operations stuff later, because on med-surg you see how much of the job is the system around the patient, not just the patient. Too many patients, not enough hands, the discharge stuck, the supplies in the wrong room. That's really what I want to work on now.
narrativeVersions.title: Mission Trail Regional - 5 West med-surg

narratives.body:
What I want next. I want to get off the bedside and into the side of healthcare where you figure out how the work should flow. I've been a nurse for twelve years and the parts I loved most were never the procedures. It was being charge and solving the puzzle, being the Epic super-user and translating between the nurses and the people building the system, and the virtual nursing pilot, where we had to invent the workflow from nothing.

So the jobs I'm looking at: clinical implementation, like an implementation specialist or clinical implementation consultant at an EHR company or a virtual care company, the person who helps a hospital or clinic actually go live and get their nurses using the thing. Or clinical operations, especially for virtual care or telehealth, running the nurse side of a virtual program, the workflows, the staffing, the metrics. Clinical informatics would be great too, I know that's harder to get into without Epic certification, but I'd take a nurse informaticist or clinical analyst role in a heartbeat if someone would sponsor the cert.

Companies that excite me are the ones doing virtual care or digital health that actually touches patients and clinicians, places like Quillfield, Bellwick, Medlattice, Dosewell, Fennel & Finch. I want a company that has nurses in the room when they decide things, not one that thinks nurses are just users.

What I don't want. I don't want to go back to full-time bedside. Part-time PRN on the side maybe, but not as my main job. I don't want sales. I've had device reps tell me I'd be great at it and I'm sure I'd make money, but I'm not carrying a quota and I'm not selling to my old coworkers. No clinical sales, no medical device sales, no "clinical account executive" that's really sales with a nursing title. And I'm not trying to become a software engineer. I took one SQL course. I like data and I'll use it, but I'm not going to be a developer and I don't want to pretend.

The hard stuff, plainly:

Pay. I need at least $95,000 base. Below that, honestly, I'm better off picking up more shifts as a nurse, so anything under $95k base is a no, I don't care how cool the company is.

Location. I live in Denver and I'm staying in Denver. Daniel's job is here and we bought a house. So it's hybrid in the Denver area or fully remote anywhere in the US. I won't relocate, and I'm not doing something that's onsite four days a week in another city either.

Travel. I can travel some, I know implementation means go-lives, but at most about 25%, so like a week a month on average. Not a road warrior job. I did that with travel nursing.

Work authorization. I'm a US citizen, so no sponsorship needed, and I don't have any kind of security clearance, I've never needed one.

Other than that I'm flexible. I'd take a step down in title if it gets me into the right company. I'd like to stay close enough to patients that I remember why it matters.
narratives.title: Goals

narratives.body:
Okay so right now I'm at Foothill Peaks Medical Center here in Denver. I'm part-time, which honestly I never thought I'd say, I was always the one picking up extra shifts. I'm 0.6, so two twelves a week, 24 hours, mostly in the ICU. It's a mixed medical-surgical ICU, and sometimes they float me to step-down when they're short, which is a lot.

How I got here. We moved up from San Antonio in March 2022 because Daniel, my partner, got a job offer here, he's a civil engineer, and it was too good for him to pass up. I'd been off work for a while at that point, after the travel nursing stuff, so the timing kind of worked out. I didn't actually start at Foothill Peaks until July 2022 because the license transfer took forever. Well, Texas and Colorado are both compact states so it shouldn't have, but there was some issue with my address change and the background check. Anyway. July 2022.

The part-time thing was on purpose. I knew I didn't want to go back to full-time bedside. I love my patients, I do, but my back, and also I think after COVID I just can't do three or four twelves a week anymore and still be a person. So I took part-time and kept the other days for figuring out what's next.

The thing I'm proudest of here honestly isn't even the nursing part. When I started, our unit's staffing was done on a paper grid and a whiteboard, and the charge nurse would be texting people at four in the morning trying to fill holes. I built a Google Sheet, a staffing grid, where the charge enters census and acuity, and it shows where we're going to be short over the next 24 hours and color codes it, red, yellow, green. My manager liked it and now she pulls it up every morning for our unit huddle. I think it saves her like an hour a day? She said that once, I didn't time it. I'd honestly say my sheet is basically how the hospital does staffing now. Which, okay, it's mostly our unit. A couple of other managers asked for a copy, but I don't know if they actually use it.

The other big thing was the virtual nursing pilot in 2024. The hospital was trying out having a nurse work remotely, from a little office with a camera and a screen in the patient rooms, doing admissions, discharge teaching, med reconciliation, all the documentation stuff, so the bedside nurses could actually be at the bedside. They picked six of us bedside nurses to pilot it and I was one of them. It was for a 28-bed med-surg unit, not my ICU. I did it for about four months, so two of my shifts a week were virtual instead of ICU. I really liked it. I liked figuring out the workflow, like what the virtual nurse owns and what the bedside nurse owns, who signs what, and we kept a shared doc of everything that was breaking. I think I wrote most of that doc, honestly. Discharge teaching got way more consistent, the bedside nurses said they had more time, and I think the discharges-before-noon number went up but I never saw the final report. The pilot ended when the grant money ran out, or that's what we were told, I'm not totally sure. They said they'd revisit it in 2026 and so far, no.

That pilot is what made me look at the operations side of healthcare. I realized I like the part where you figure out how the work should flow more than I like doing the twelfth bath of the night. Sorry, that sounds bad. You know what I mean.

So last September, September 2025, I started the Google Data Analytics certificate. Spreadsheets, SQL, a bit of R which I did not love, Tableau, and I ended up doing my capstone in Looker Studio because it was free and easy to share. I finished in June 2026. For the capstone I did a staffing ratio dashboard, nurse-to-patient ratios by shift against census and acuity, on made-up data, because obviously I can't use real patient stuff. It's on my GitHub. It's not fancy, but I actually understand what a join is now, which a year ago, no way.

Oh, and I'm on the unit practice council here, we meet once a month, I've been on it since 2023. We redid how we do bedside shift report, that was most of last year. That's about it for here, I think.

narratives.body:
My first job out of school. I graduated with my BSN in May 2014 from Bexar Valley College of Nursing, passed boards that July, and started at Mission Trail Regional Medical Center in August 2014 in their new grad residency. They put me on 5 West, which is a 32-bed med-surg unit. Mostly medical, some post-op, lots of COPD and heart failure and diabetic foot stuff, and a lot of elderly patients who fall. I did nights the whole first year because that's what new grads got.

Ratios were one to five on days and one to six on nights, sometimes seven when someone called out, which was a lot. Honestly med-surg is where you learn time management or you drown. I learned to chart fast and prioritize. I also learned I was really bad at saying no to people, which, still working on it.

The thing from 5 West I'd actually put on paper is the falls work. Our unit had one of the worst fall rates in the hospital, and in 2015 I joined the unit falls committee. It was me, two other nurses, a tech, and our nurse manager would come sometimes. We did hourly rounding with a script, the four Ps, pain, potty, position, possessions, and we got the bed alarms actually turned on, because people were turning them off since they went off all the time, and the yellow socks and wristbands for high-risk patients. I made the hourly rounding log that went on the door. Falls went down, I think from like five a month to two or three, I don't remember exactly, our manager had the numbers. It's not like we fixed falls forever, but it was better.

I also precepted. After my first year they had me precept new grads, and I precepted six of them between 2015 and 2016. I liked it a lot. I was basically the unit educator for a while there. Well, not officially, we had an actual clinical educator for 5 West and a couple of other units, she ran the skills fairs and the competencies, but she was spread really thin so I helped her with the skills fair once and people came to me with questions. I liked being the person people asked.

I got moved to days in 2015, I think that summer. Days were busier but I had more interaction with the doctors and case management and that's where I first got a feel for discharges and bed flow, like why a patient who's medically ready to go still sits there for two days waiting on a nursing home bed. That stuff always frustrated me. Nobody owned it.

I left 5 West in June 2016 to go to the MICU. I'd been wanting ICU since school, and the hospital had an internal ICU internship, a few months of classes and precepted shifts, so I applied and got in. My manager on 5 West was sad, she said she'd hoped I'd go into charge there. But I wanted the ICU.

Looking back, med-surg gave me the basics. And honestly I think it made me good at the operations stuff later, because on med-surg you see how much of the job is the system around the patient, not just the patient. Too many patients, not enough hands, the discharge stuck, the supplies in the wrong room. That's really what I want to work on now.

We're looking for a Clinical Operations Manager to run the day-to-day operations of Virtual Care Nursing. You'll own staffing and scheduling, workflow design, quality and performance metrics, and the tools our nurses use every day. What you'll do

- Own the staffing model for Virtual Care Nursing: forecast demand by hour and day, build schedules, and adjust coverage when volume spikes.
- Design and document clinical workflows for triage, post-discharge follow-up and outreach programs; make sure nurses know who owns what and when to escalate.
- Define, track and report operational and quality metrics such as response times, triage accuracy, follow-up completion and member satisfaction.
- Lead quality improvement projects using clear baselines and targets; audit charts and share results with the team.
- Partner with product and engineering to improve the tools nurses use; translate frontline feedback into clear requirements and test new features before launch.

- Make sure workflows meet clinical policy, licensure and regulatory requirements across states.
- Support launches of new clinical programs, including training and go-live support.

What you bring

- Active RN license; compact license required, with willingness to obtain additional state licenses as needed (we cover the cost).
- 7+ years of clinical nursing experience, including acute care.
- 2+ years of leadership experience, such as charge nurse, team lead, unit supervisor or nurse manager.
- Experience running a quality improvement or process improvement project with measurable results.
- Comfort with data: you can build and read a dashboard, work in spreadsheets, and use metrics to make staffing and workflow decisions.
- Experience with EHR systems and introducing new clinical tools to staff.
- Clear writing; you can turn a messy workflow into a one-page guide.

- SQL, Looker or Tableau experience.
- Experience as an EHR super-user or trainer.

Compensation

Dear Hiring Team,

I can bring the view from both sides of a go-live to Quillfield Health's hospital implementation team: I have trained the nurses before launch, stood at their elbows during it, and worked inside a virtual nursing pilot. Your posting asks for a nurse who knows what makes bedside staff adopt a new tool or quietly work around it. That is the experience I have.

I then gave three weeks of at-the-elbow support and kept an issue log of about 150 workflow challenges and build defects, so I could follow each one to a resolution by the command center. For a year after launch, I brought change requests from my unit to the clinical informatics team in monthly optimization meetings.

At Foothill Peaks Medical Center, I was one of six bedside nurses piloting virtual nursing on a 28-bed med-surg unit. I ran remote admissions, medication reconciliations and discharge teaching, and I wrote most of the pilot's shared workflow documentation. That work gave me practice at defining what the virtual nurse does and what the nurse at the bedside does, which is the center of the role you describe.

As a charge nurse, I co-led a sepsis initiative that raised SEP-1 bundle compliance from 58% to 86% over nine months. We set up nurse-driven screening, put reference cards at the bedside and audited 20 charts a month. I also worked with the clinical informatics team to cut how often the Epic sepsis alert fired, so the alerts nurses saw were ones they could act on. On the data side, I built a staffing dashboard in Looker Studio, fed by a BigQuery SQL pipeline, so I am comfortable building a tracker and explaining what it shows to a nurse leader.

I would welcome a conversation about how this experience could help your clients through their first 90 days. Thank you for your time.

Renata Alvarez

Clinical Implementation Specialist (RN) at Quillfield Health · Remote (US)

Clinical Implementation Specialist (RN)
Quillfield Health
Location: Remote (US)
Employment type: Full-time

About Quillfield Health

Quillfield Health is a whole-person virtual care company. We work with health systems, health plans, employers and individuals to make care easier to get, from urgent care and primary care to chronic condition management and mental health. Our hospital and health system solutions bring virtual care into the places clinicians already work: telehealth carts and devices in patient rooms, virtual sitting, virtual nursing, and connected specialty consults.

About the role

Our Hospital & Health System Implementation team gets new client programs live and working. As a Clinical Implementation Specialist, you'll be the clinical voice on the implementation team for hospital customers launching virtual care programs, such as virtual nursing, virtual sitting and tele-critical care. You'll partner with a project manager and a technical implementation engineer, and you'll own the clinical side: workflow design, training, go-live support and the first 90 days of adoption.

This role is for a nurse who has lived through a go-live from the unit side and knows what makes bedside staff adopt a new tool, or quietly work around it.

What you'll do

- Lead clinical discovery sessions with nursing leaders, unit managers and frontline staff to understand current-state workflows for admissions, discharges, patient observation and rounding.
- Design future-state workflows that define what the virtual clinician owns and what the bedside clinician owns, and document them in clear workflow maps and role guides.
- Build and deliver training for client nurses, charge nurses and virtual staff, including train-the-trainer and super-user programs.
- Provide on-site and remote go-live support, including at-the-elbow support on units during launch weeks.
- Track and triage go-live issues; separate training gaps from configuration problems and route them to the right team.
- Define adoption and outcome measures with the client (for example virtual admission completion, discharge education completion, time to discharge) and review them with client leadership at 30, 60 and 90 days.
- Feed what you learn from the field back to our product and clinical teams.
- Keep implementation plans, risks and decisions up to date in our project tools.

What you bring

- Active, unrestricted RN license (compact license preferred).
- 5+ years of acute care nursing experience; critical care, step-down or med-surg strongly preferred.
- Experience with at least one EHR implementation, upgrade or major optimization, as a super-user, trainer, informatics nurse or project team member.
- Experience teaching adults, such as precepting, unit education, super-user training or classroom training.
- Comfort leading meetings with nurse managers and directors and holding your ground on workflow decisions.
- Strong organization: you can run several client launches at different stages without dropping details.
- Working comfort with spreadsheets and basic data; you can build a tracker and summarize what it shows.

Nice to have

- Charge nurse or other unit leadership experience.
- Experience with virtual nursing, virtual sitting, tele-ICU or other telehealth programs.
- Familiarity with Epic or Oracle Health (Cerner) inpatient workflows.
- Data analytics coursework or experience with SQL, Looker, Tableau or similar.
- Quality improvement project experience (falls, sepsis, CLABSI, CAUTI or similar).

Travel

This role travels to client sites for discovery and go-live, up to 20% on average. Travel is concentrated around launches; some months will have none.

Compensation

The base salary range for this role is $98,000 to $124,000 per year. Placement in the range depends on experience and location. This role is also eligible for an annual bonus and our benefits, including medical, dental and vision coverage, a 401(k) with company match, paid time off and paid parental leave.

Work authorization

Candidates must be authorized to work in the United States. We are not able to sponsor visas for this role.

Quillfield Health is an equal opportunity employer. We welcome applicants of all backgrounds and do not discriminate on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, age, disability, veteran status or any other protected characteristic.

We're looking for a Clinical Operations Manager to run the day-to-day operations of Virtual Care Nursing. You'll own staffing and scheduling, workflow design, quality and performance metrics, and the tools our nurses use every day. You'll manage a group of nurse team leads and partner closely with our medical directors, product managers and data team.

- Own the staffing model for Virtual Care Nursing: forecast demand by hour and day, build schedules, and adjust coverage when volume spikes.

This role is fully remote within the US. Occasional travel for team meetings, about two to four trips a year (under 10%).
